4. Merge eligibility rules


4.1 Exact duplicates


Exact duplicates SHOULD be merged into a single active object with preserved provenance multiplicity.


4.2 Semantic duplicates

6. Family-specific rules


6.1 TextAtom


TextAtoms MAY be merged when normalized meaning is materially identical and scope is aligned.


They MUST NOT be merged across:

Boundary
Reason

6.2 EvidenceAtom


EvidenceAtoms SHOULD usually remain distinct unless they are byte-for-byte or span-for-span identical. Multiple independent evidence spans that support the same claim are better stored as multiple evidence atoms linked to a common claim.


6.3 PolicyAtom


PolicyAtoms SHOULD be merged conservatively. Even subtle wording changes MAY carry normative consequences. If two policies differ in modal force, exception structure, or applicability, they MUST remain distinct.


6.4 CodeAtom


CodeAtoms MUST NOT be merged merely because they are similar in behavior. Exact payload identity and stable content-addressed equivalence are required for hard merge. Otherwise they MAY be clustered as similar implementations or linked through refinement or supersession.


6.5 AnalysisAtom family


Analytical objects SHOULD be merged only when the same analysis type, scope, method, and finding meaning coincide closely. Findings from different analysis runs SHOULD typically remain distinct but MAY be linked or superseded.


7. Provenance preservation


Every merge action MUST preserve provenance multiplicity.


7.1 Provenance rule


When multiple candidates merge into one canonical object, the canonical object MUST retain references to all source and transformation lineages that contributed to the merge.

1. Purpose


The portal projection layer provides human-usable and tool-usable views over the atomic substrate without treating those views as primary storage truth. It materializes stable, intelligible workspace views from content-addressed objects, graph relations, and recipes.


2. Projection thesis


The substrate stores atoms and immutable content objects. Users and tools often need familiar workspace projections: project trees, file-like structures, documentation bundles, trace reports, code views, and assembled artifacts.

1 Supersession Policy v1


Document ID: uaks_v1_supersession_policy_20260311


1.1 Purpose


Supersession defines how atoms are replaced when knowledge evolves.


Atoms are never overwritten. Instead a new atom replaces the old one via a relation.


old_atom  →  IS_SUPERSEDED_BY  →  new_atom


This preserves the complete knowledge history.



1.2 Supersession triggers


Supersession occurs when:

Trigger
Example
policy revision
rule updated
factual correction

analysis refinement
improved analytical interpretation
code revision
function implementation changed
ontology revision
classification corrected


1.3 Supersession requirements


A valid supersession requires:

Requirement
Meaning
new atom created
old atom preserved
relation recorded
explicit supersession edge
provenance recorded
reason for replacement
timestamp
time of change
reviewer validation
if high-impact


1.4 Supersession chain


Supersession chains form temporal lineage.


Atom A (2024)
   ↓ superseded_by
Atom B (2025)
   ↓ superseded_by
Atom C (2026)


Assemblies default to latest accepted atom.


Historical views may access older atoms.



1.5 Supersession safety rules


Assemblies MUST NOT:


mix superseded atoms with current atoms

hide supersession chains

discard historical atoms

1 Hashing Standard v1


Document ID: uaks_v1_hashing_standard_20260311


1.1 Purpose


Every atomic object must have a content-derived identifier.


The identifier is a cryptographic fingerprint of the atom’s canonical form.


This guarantees:


immutability

reproducibility

deduplication



1.2 Hash algorithm


The system uses:


SHA-256


Reasons:

Property
Benefit
deterministic
same input produces same ID
collision resistance
prevents identity conflicts
industry standard
widely supported


1.3 Atom identifier structure


atom:<hash>


Example


atom:7fa9c1c9c8d23a...



1.4 Hash input specification


The hash MUST be calculated from the atom’s canonical payload.


Canonical payload includes:

Field
Included

yes

yes

yes
whitespace

Excluded:

Field
Reason

would change identity

reviewer ID

from pathlib import Path

def walk(path: Path, prefix: str = ""):
    entries = sorted([p for p in path.iterdir()], key=lambda p: (p.is_file(), p.name))
    for i, entry in enumerate(entries):
        connector = "└── " if i == len(entries) - 1 else "├── "
        print(prefix + connector + entry.name)
        if entry.is_dir():
            extension = "    " if i == len(entries) - 1 else "│   "
            walk(entry, prefix + extension)

root = Path(".")
print(root.resolve().name)
walk(root)
EOF

Short answer: features are not locked. In a system like the one you are building, evolution is not just allowed—it is an explicit design property of the architecture. The specification phase does not freeze behavior permanently; it establishes stable invariants while allowing controlled evolution around them.


The key distinction is between structural invariants and implementation features.



1. What Actually Becomes “Locked”


In a mature architecture like the one you just defined, only a small set of things should become highly stable.


These are the substrate invariants.


Structural invariants


These should change very rarely.


They include:


Atom identity model
Content-addressable persistence
Graph-based relation substrate
Supersession instead of overwrite
Provenance requirements
Separation of evidence / knowledge / analysis


These are the laws of physics of the system.


Changing them later is possible but extremely expensive because every stored atom depends on them.


So the goal of the specification phase was to lock these primitives, not the entire system.



2. What Is Expected to Evolve


Everything else should evolve continuously.


Examples include:


Refinery algorithms
AST extraction improvements
embedding models
assembly heuristics
ontology expansion
analysis integration
ranking methods
UI / portal behavior
schema extensions


These are policy layers, not substrate laws.


They are expected to change.



3. The Architectural Pattern You Just Defined


The architecture deliberately supports evolution through four mechanisms.


Content-addressed identity


Nothing is overwritten.


New versions simply create new atoms.


So improvements never destroy history.



Supersession chains


Knowledge evolves like this:


old_atom
   ↓
superseded_by
   ↓
new_atom


This allows the system to improve without destabilizing earlier states.



Assembly recipes


Outputs are not stored permanently.


They are re-rendered from atoms.


This means improving the refinery or ontology automatically improves outputs.



Parallel analytical lanes


New analysis systems can be added without rewriting the core.


Example:


knowledge base
     │
     ├─ linguistic analysis
     ├─ code static analysis
     ├─ runtime telemetry
     ├─ ontology inference


Each produces atoms through the same normalization membrane.



4. The Real Lock Point


What becomes stable is the interface between layers, not the layers themselves.

Those systems have evolved for decades because they froze core primitives, not features.


Your system should follow the same rule:


Stable substrate, evolving machinery.

This charter defines the canonical metadata, identity, frontmatter, registry, and synchronization model for UAKS-v1.

Assessment


I think the repository is a strong and unusually complete v0/v1, but it is still fundamentally a document-and-message indexing system with atomization features, not yet a full atomic knowledge operating system in the stricter sense you are now aiming for.


What is already good is substantial. The repo has a real ingestion layer, multiple source adapters, a chunking/atomization layer, SQLite FTS5, ChromaDB-backed semantic search, hybrid retrieval via reciprocal-rank fusion, an LLM extraction layer, a graph layer, a web UI, and a large CLI surface. It is not vapor; it is a working substrate. The README describes nine source adapters, a federated indexer, hybrid FTS/vector search, relationship detection, and a presentation layer with REST, WebSocket, React, and 30+ CLI commands. The package metadata also shows a serious TypeScript monorepo with workspaces, Playwright, better-sqlite3, ChromaDB, Express, Vitest, and multiple runtime/probe scripts. GitHub+4GitHub+4GitHub+4


The more important question is whether it is architecturally aligned with your newer “atomic assembler” target. My answer is: partially aligned, but not yet structurally resolved.


What I think is strong


The project already solves a real problem. The README frames the failure mode correctly: AI conversations are trapped in vendor UIs, stored as monolithic blobs, poorly searchable across sessions, and not analytically mined for implicit knowledge. That diagnosis is good, and the system addresses it with concrete subsystems rather than hand-waving. GitHub


The retrieval stack is also solid for its stage. SQLite FTS5 for exact retrieval plus ChromaDB for semantic retrieval plus RRF fusion is a rational architecture for a personal or small-team knowledge system. The README explicitly describes FTS5 on title, content, context, and tags, vector collections per embedding profile, and rank fusion with configurable weights. GitHub+1


The federated ingestion direction is correct. Pulling from chat exports, browser automation, local files, Google Docs, Apple Notes, and bookmarks is exactly the kind of breadth an actual personal knowledge substrate needs. GitHub


There is also evidence that you were already feeling toward operational rigor rather than toy scripting. The package scripts include reindex evidence capture, preflight probes, alert verification, redaction commands, release evidence generation, and multiple test suites. That is atypically disciplined for a personal knowledge project. GitHub


Where it falls short relative to your current theory


The biggest limitation is that your current “atom” is still too close to a chunk, message, or snippet, rather than a governed semantic primitive.


The code shows that conversation atomization is primarily message-level, with each message turned into one unit if it is longer than 20 characters, and code blocks extracted via a regex over fenced markdown. Type inference is heuristic, based on keyword checks like question marks, function, class, should we, and so on. That is effective as pragmatic ingestion, but it is not yet true semantic atomization. It will overproduce coarse units, misclassify roles, and miss internal logical structure. GitHub


The database schema is another tell. atomic_units stores title, content, context, category, tags, keywords, and optional embeddings, plus provenance fields such as conversation_id and document_id. That is enough for search and light relationshiping, but it is not yet enough for the stronger model you described later: immutable atom identity, supersession chains, evidence spans, state mutations, content hashes, formal parent/child abstraction relations, contradiction state, assembly recipes, or executable code primitives. GitHub


The relationship layer is better than average, but still secondary rather than foundational. The README says candidate relationships are first selected by vector similarity and then typed by an LLM into categories like references, builds_on, contradicts, and implements. That is useful, but it means relationships are still mostly inferred after the fact rather than encoded as first-class structural commitments during refining. GitHub+1


In other words, the repo is good at ingesting, indexing, extracting, and surfacing, but not yet at storing truth as atomic, version-aware, composition-ready units.


The deepest architectural issue


Your present system treats atomization mostly as a processing tactic. Your newer theory treats atomization as the primary ontology.


That difference matters.


In the current repo, a conversation or document is still the dominant source object, and atoms are generated from it for downstream search. In the stronger architecture, the atom becomes the primary persistent object, while conversations, files, summaries, notes, and views become derivative assemblies. The repo has already moved in that direction, but it has not crossed that threshold.


What I would improve first


1. Redefine the atom schema


This is the highest-value change.


Your current unit shape is roughly: text snippet + tags + category + provenance + optional relationships. The next version should split this into explicit first-class atom types.


At minimum, I would introduce:


TextAtom
CodeAtom
EvidenceAtom
PolicyAtom
RelationAtom
RecipeAtom


Each should have immutable IDs and content hashes. Each should also carry explicit provenance spans, validation state, temporal scope, and supersession pointers. Right now the schema is more like “searchable unit storage.” You want “truth-bearing semantic object storage.” The current schema does not yet encode that distinction. GitHub+1


2. Replace heuristic conversation atomization with proposition extraction


The message-level pass is too coarse. One assistant message can contain multiple insights, a decision, a caveat, and an example. The current logic largely turns that into one unit plus optionally one regex-extracted code block. GitHub


The improved refinery should do proposition splitting. One message should be decomposed into multiple atomic claims or procedures where warranted. That means extracting declarative propositions, decision rationales, assumptions, action items, evidence references, and code references separately.


Your present atomizer is a good bootstrapper. It is not yet a canonical refinery.


3. Stop treating code as fenced text


This is the clearest place where your new feature should change the system.


At the moment, code extraction in conversations is regex-based over fenced blocks. That is useful, but it means code is being treated as decorated text rather than executable structure. GitHub


Your next version should add a separate code refinery that parses source via AST and emits CodeAtom objects for functions, methods, classes, modules, schemas, tests, and configuration primitives. Those objects should include signature, dependencies, runtime, side-effect profile, complexity score, content hash, and call-graph links.


This should be built within the same overall ontology but as a separate refinery path.


4. Introduce explicit evidence and provenance spans


Your system already has provenance fields like conversationId, documentId, and parentSectionId, and the README mentions redaction metadata and document hierarchy. That is a strong start. GitHub


But for the system you now want, provenance must become more exact. Every atom should be able to say not merely “I came from conversation X,” but “I came from message 14, characters 220–497,” or “I was distilled from code file Y, AST node Z, commit hash H.” Without that, you can retrieve and summarize, but you cannot really audit, dispute, or confidently propagate changes.


5. Add supersession and recipe persistence


Your current schema looks snapshot-oriented rather than mutation-aware. I did not see first-class supersession chains or recipe objects in the surfaced schema. GitHub


You need both.


Supersession lets an atom be replaced without ambiguity. Recipe persistence lets a successful assembled output be stored as an ordered list of atom IDs plus template parameters, instead of frozen text. That is how you make the same underlying atomic substrate regenerate updated documents automatically.


6. Move relationships from “detected links” to “structural bonds”


Right now your relationship detection is valuable, but it is closer to semantic annotation than formal composition. GitHub+1


For the next architecture, some relationships should be inferred, but many should be structural and typed at creation time. For example:


A policy atom governs a requirement atom.
A requirement atom is_implemented_by a code atom.
A code atom is_verified_by a test atom.
A document atom summarizes a recipe atom.
A deprecated atom is_superseded_by a newer atom.


That is closer to the bonding logic you described.


My judgment on the repo as a foundation


I would not discard this repo. I would treat it as a valuable precursor system.


It already proves several things:


The ingestion problem is real and partially solved.
The search stack is viable.
The CLI and web presentation concepts are viable.
The project has operational seriousness.
The atomization concept is not imaginary.


What it does not yet prove is that the current storage model can cleanly evolve into your stricter atomic/coded/recipe/CAS architecture without a schema break. I suspect it can evolve, but not without a substantial v2 refactor.


How I would evolve it


I would take a strangler-fig approach, not a full rewrite.


Create a new v2 atom schema alongside the current one.
Keep the existing ingestion and search surfaces alive.
Add a new refinement pipeline that produces TextAtomV2, CodeAtomV2, and EvidenceAtomV2.
Introduce content hashes and supersession edges.
Add a recipe table.
Add exact provenance spans.
Then progressively shift search and assembly to the v2 objects.


That approach preserves the working parts while letting you harden the ontology.


The single most important conceptual shift


Right now the project is optimized for the question:


“How do I search and extract value from my conversations and documents?”


Your newer theory is optimized for the question:


“How do I persist knowledge and logic as atomic, recomposable, version-aware primitives from which all outputs are assembled?”


That is not a small feature addition. It is a change in system center of gravity.


Bottom line


My view is:


This is a serious, intelligent, worthwhile build.
It is ahead of most personal knowledge projects.
It already contains several of the right instincts.
But it is still one architectural layer short of the system you now actually want.


It is best understood as:


A strong retrieval-and-extraction precursor to an atomic knowledge operating system.


Not the final form, but absolutely a usable foundation.

documents are no longer primary storage objects

Atomic units become the persistent substrate.

Yes — design for it now


That parallel linguistic-analysis system should not be treated as an external convenience. It should be treated as a first-class upstream producer in the overall architecture.


If you do not design for it now, you will later end up with one of two bad outcomes:


First, the linguistic system will dump opaque reports into the knowledge base as dead documents, which recreates the very monolith problem you are trying to escape.


Second, you will over-couple the new knowledge base to the internal assumptions of the linguistic system, which will make both harder to evolve.


The correct design is a federated atomic intake model:


external analysis system produces structured findings → translation layer converts them into governed atoms → new knowledge base stores them as linked, typed, provenance-rich objects


So the answer is yes: this absolutely needs to be designed for, and it should be designed as a formal integration lane, not an ad hoc import feature.



What it should look like conceptually


You now have three distinct domains:

Domain
What it contains
What it is good at
Source domain
raw conversations, documents, notes, code, media-derived text
primary evidence
Linguistic-analysis domain
token patterns, syntax, rhetoric, discourse, semantic drift, ontology extraction, motif recurrence, style signatures
interpretation and structural analysis
Knowledge-base domain
durable atoms, relations, recipes, provenance, assembly, cross-domain retrieval
long-term governed memory

The linguistic-analysis system should therefore be treated neither as raw evidence nor as final truth.


It is a derivative analytical instrument.


That means its outputs should enter the new system in a distinct ontological class, somewhere between evidence and interpretation.



The key design principle


Do not import linguistic-analysis outputs as plain text reports.


Instead, import them as structured analytical products that can be decomposed into atomic findings.


The integration model should be:

   ↓

   ↓
Assembly-ready knowledge substrate


The crucial piece is the translation / normalization layer. That is the membrane between systems.


Without that membrane, the knowledge base gets polluted with foreign assumptions, foreign schemas, and ungoverned interpretation objects.

These outputs should not all be treated the same way. Some are more like evidence, some more like interpretation, some more like proposed ontology, and some more like diagnostics.


So the knowledge base must distinguish them formally.



What new atom types you need


To support this, I would extend the v2 ontology with a specific analysis lane.


At minimum, add these atom classes:

Atom type
Purpose
AnalysisAtom
a normalized analytical finding
ObservationAtom
lower-level pattern directly observed from a corpus
InterpretationAtom
an inferential conclusion derived from observations
MetricAtom
numeric output from the linguistic system
TaxonomyProposalAtom
proposed category, cluster, or concept grouping
SignatureAtom
persistent stylistic or structural pattern
DriftAtom
a change-over-time pattern in language or meaning
AnalysisRunAtom
metadata about one execution of the external analysis pipeline

These should be distinct from ordinary TextAtom, CodeAtom, and EvidenceAtom.


That matters because a sentence in a source conversation and a sentence produced by a linguistic-analysis engine are not the same kind of object.


One is source evidence. The other is analytical output about that source.



Provenance model for the parallel system


This is where most systems fail.


You need two-layer provenance at minimum, ideally three-layer provenance.


Layer 1: source provenance


What raw corpus was analyzed?


For example:


conversation IDs
document IDs
time windows
author scopes
project scopes
code scopes
selection filters


Layer 2: analysis provenance


What exact analytical run produced the result?


For example:


analysis engine name
version
prompt or model config
algorithm class
parameters
dictionary / ontology versions
timestamp
confidence method


Layer 3: transformation provenance


How was the external result translated into the knowledge base?


For example:


normalization rules
schema version
import job ID
conflict-resolution logic
deduplication outcome


This gives you traceability from final stored finding back to both the raw source and the analytical mechanism that produced it.


Without this, analytical outputs become untrustworthy very quickly.



How the integration should work architecturally


The cleanest model is a publish-normalize-ingest pattern.


1. Publish


The linguistic-analysis system should export structured result bundles, not prose-only summaries.


Those bundles should be machine-readable and stable.


The export object should contain:


run metadata
corpus scope
findings
metrics
links back to source spans
confidence values
proposed relations
optional embeddings
optional cluster identifiers


2. Normalize


A dedicated integration service reads the export and maps it to the knowledge-base ontology.


This service should:


resolve source references
convert external identifiers to internal identifiers
separate observations from interpretations
assign atom classes
add validation state
merge duplicates
record provenance
generate relation edges


3. Ingest


The normalized output is stored as first-class atoms and linked into the broader graph.


At this stage the system can connect:


analysis findings to source evidence
analysis findings to text atoms
analysis findings to code atoms
analysis findings to prior analyses
analysis findings to recipes and assemblies



The data contract you should define now


You need an explicit contract between the external linguistic system and the new knowledge base.


This does not need to be technologically fancy at first, but it must be semantically strict.


The external system should never “just send a paragraph.”


It should send something like a structured analytical envelope with fields equivalent to:

Field
Meaning
analysis_run_id
unique ID for one run
analysis_type
discourse, semantic drift, syntax, rhetoric, etc.
source_scope
what corpus or slice was analyzed
finding_id
stable ID for each exported finding
finding_kind
observation, interpretation, metric, taxonomy proposal, signature
finding_text
normalized human-readable statement
evidence_refs
source spans or source atom IDs
confidence
numeric or categorical confidence
method
algorithm/model/process used
timestamp
when produced
supersedes
prior finding if applicable
tags
ontology or domain tags
relations
explicit suggested edges to internal objects

That contract is what allows the two systems to evolve independently.



How to prevent contamination of the core knowledge base


You do not want every analytical output immediately treated as stable truth.


So you need a trust gradient.


I recommend the following validation states for imported analysis objects:

State
Meaning
imported
accepted from external system, not yet reviewed
machine-derived
known to be analysis-generated
reviewed
checked by human or trusted adjudicator
accepted
allowed in normal assembly for standard outputs
experimental
visible only in exploratory or research contexts
disputed
challenged or contradicted
deprecated
superseded by newer or better analysis

This keeps the analytical lane useful without letting it silently rewrite the ontology.



The most important relation types


To make the parallel system genuinely useful, define these edge types from the start.

Relation
Meaning
analyzes
analysis object analyzes a source or atom
derived_from
finding comes from a source span or atom set
supports
finding strengthens another atom or interpretation
contradicts
finding conflicts with another atom or interpretation
proposes_taxonomy_for
analysis proposes ontology over a corpus
detects_drift_in
identifies change over time in an entity, topic, or style
characterizes
gives a structural description of an entity/corpus/project
maps_to
aligns an external analysis label to an internal concept
requires_review_of
flags atom or code object for re-evaluation
is_superseded_by
analysis result replaced by newer run

These edges are what convert “interesting reports” into operational knowledge.



How this becomes practically useful


Once integrated correctly, the linguistic-analysis system can do more than annotate language. It becomes a trigger system for knowledge maintenance.


Examples:


A semantic-drift finding can indicate that a concept has changed meaning across a project over six months, which should trigger taxonomy review.


A rhetoric-pattern finding can reveal that a set of memos consistently mixes instruction and speculation, which should trigger atom reclassification.


A business-rule language shift can be linked to code atoms implementing that rule, which should trigger impact analysis.


A motif recurrence analysis can identify latent conceptual clusters across notes, which can seed new ontology branches.


A discourse-structure analysis can produce reusable recipes for assembling future reports in the style that best matches the corpus.


That is when the external analytical system stops being “another report generator” and becomes a genuine co-processor for the knowledge OS.



Whether this should be synchronous or asynchronous


Architecturally, this should usually be asynchronous at the system level, even though conceptually it is parallel.


The linguistic system should run on its own cadence and publish result bundles.


The knowledge base should ingest those bundles through a controlled pipeline.


That keeps the systems decoupled and resilient.


However, the knowledge base should also support on-demand federation, meaning an assembly or query can ask:


“show me source atoms plus the latest accepted linguistic analyses relevant to this topic”


So the systems are operationally decoupled but logically composable.



Recommended structural pattern


The cleanest pattern is this:


Core substrate


Stores source atoms, code atoms, evidence atoms, recipes, and accepted analysis atoms.


External analysis exchange layer


Receives export bundles from the linguistic-analysis system.


Normalization membrane


Maps foreign results into local ontology and trust states.


Analytical graph lane


Stores imported analysis runs and findings as a distinct subgraph.


Assembly policy layer


Determines when analytical findings are included in normal outputs, exploratory outputs, or deep-research outputs.


That gives you a separation between memory, analysis, and rendering.



What I would explicitly design now


I would design five things immediately.


1. A foreign-analysis import schema


This is the contract for analytical result bundles.


2. New atom classes for derivative analysis


Without these, the system will flatten evidence and interpretation together.


3. A provenance model for analysis runs


You will need this sooner than you think.


4. A trust and validation policy


So imported analysis does not silently become canon.


5. A relation vocabulary for cross-system linking


This is what makes the integration operational instead of decorative.



My recommendation


Yes, design for this now.


But do not design it as “another source adapter.”


Design it as a parallel analytical producer with a formal exchange contract and a protected ontology boundary.


That is the right abstraction.


In one line:


the new knowledge base should ingest not just sources, but also governed interpretations of sources
